title: Introduction
paragraphs:
Chapter 1
Introduction
Chapter abstract. This chapter introduces the problem: social-media radio shapes
what students hear, trust, and learn, yet platform design and audience measurement
are usually studied separately. It states the research questions, objectives, hypotheses,
scope, and the evidence hierarchy used throughout. It explains why a measured eld
wave is combined with a calibrated in-silico experiment rather than a real platform
trial, and it denes the contribution: an EST-based design framework, a transparent
measurement model, and a reproducible testbed. It closes with the structure of the
thesis.
1.1
Background and Motivation
Internet distribution and social networking connect audio production with new
forms of discovery, circulation, and audience response. The scholarly question is
not whether these technologies are uniformly benecial or harmful, but how specic
arrangements change what people encounter and how they evaluate it (Spinelli &
Dann, 2019; Sullivan, 2019).
Evidence about misinformation and algorithmic selection motivates the in-
quiry without resolving it.
Vosoughi et al.
(2018) analyse true and false news

circulation on Twitter; their result is not a universal law governing every audio net-
work. Gauthier et al. (2026) identify some eects of feed assignment but not uniform
changes across political outcomes. These ndings support examining architecture
while requiring careful outcome denitions and contextual limits.
The present thesis develops Epistemic Systems Theory (EST), species the
LOKLOK platform, and examines audience evaluations in a journey-related listen-
ing setting. It links a eld questionnaire to a separate calibrated simulation. The
aim is a defensible account of the relationships among architecture, judgments, and
measurement, rather than an assumption that a positive rating demonstrates accu-
rate content or successful learning.
1.2
From Internet Radio to Social Media Radio
Internet delivery, radio programming, on-demand access, and social networking de-
scribe dierent properties. A station can stream a linear programme without listener
proles. A podcast can be downloaded without a social feed. A social network can
carry an audio clip without a continuous radio service.
Treating these as inter-
changeable would obscure the study's population and the architectural intervention
it proposes.
Rime et al. (2022) examine podcasting through tensions rather than a single
xed technological denition. Sullivan (2019) distinguishes the storage, discovery,
and consumption functions of podcast platforms.
An episode may therefore be
hosted in one place, discovered through a social post, and heard through another in-
terface. Table 1.1 gives this thesis's working classication, not a universal taxonomy

1.2.1
Broadcasting and Social Circulation
A host can post an episode, a listener can circulate an extract, and others can com-
ment, challenge, or recommend it. Spinelli and Dann (2019) discuss audio produc-
tion and relationships with listeners in podcasting. This supports examining radio
as more than a transmitterreceiver pair, but does not imply equal participation or
improved information merely because interaction is possible.
This thesis distinguishes editorial selection, platform selection, and listener
selection. Editorial selection determines what is recorded and how claims are framed.
Platform selection determines which posts become visible.
Listener selection in-
cludes choosing, replaying, ignoring, and sharing. EST concerns the relationship
among these stages. Assigning all three to an abstract algorithm would obscure
responsibility and prevent a precise explanation of eects.

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION
4
1.2.2
Why Social Media Radio Matters
The form brings together voice-based communication, networked circulation, and
visible audience metrics. It therefore oers a setting for studying how trust in a
speaker relates to trust in a message and how metrics aect visibility. Student par-
ticipation can also involve questioning, sourcing, production, and correction. These
are opportunities motivating the research, not ndings that the present respondents
acquired those capabilities.
The same aordances create risks. An extract can omit qualications in a
longer programme; popularity can become a credibility cue; and a correction may
reach a dierent audience from the original post. Access depends on connectivity,
devices, language, and accessible interfaces. Greater technical reach is not equivalent
to equitable participation, and audio convenience is not equivalent to sustained
attention. Transcripts and source links could support review, but their availability
and use require separate measurement.
Listening context matters. Groot Kormelink et al. (2025) found that re-
peated news-podcast use was organised around particular everyday routines. The
journey setting here is therefore a concrete reception context, not grounds for as-
suming that commuters are uniformly attentive or distracted. Journey duration and
reported interaction remain contextual variables until listening time and attention
are independently measured.

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION
5
1.2.3
Why a Radio-Specic Case Rather Than Generic Social Media
The thesis does not claim that social media radio is a representative sample of all
social media. It uses social media radio as a bounded, mechanism-oriented case in
which the propositions of EST can be specied, manipulated, and measured without
conating modality with architecture. The distinction is a scope condition, not a
rhetorical preference.
Three features make the case scientically productive. First, radio-like au-
dio is voice-centred and temporally organised. A listener encounters a programmed
stream or an episode, not an undierentiated multimodal feed. This makes broad-
caster identity, vocal presence, sequence, and repair observable, and it gives engage-
ment a behavioural referent (continued listening, replay, interaction) rather than a
generic click. Second, the form combines editorial selection with platform selection
and listener selection (Section 1.2). That combination allows the BRS, diversity-
constrained recommendation, echo control, and correction to be varied as separate
architectural levers. Third, the eld population and instrument are dened for this
setting: university students listening to social media radio during a ride, rating
broadcaster credibility, perceived benet, and their own media competence. The
outcome semantics therefore match the stimulus.
A generic social media design would weaken identication in four ways. (i)
Modality and architecture would co-vary: text, image, video, short-form, live, and
ranked feeds bundle dierent attention regimes, production costs, and credibility
cues. (ii) Outcome measures would not be construct-equivalent: a like, a watch
time, a completed listen, and a credibility rating are not interchangeable. (iii) The

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION
6
treatment set would be underidentied: many platform features would change at
once, so a contrast could not be attributed to the BRS, diversity, or echo control.
(iv) External validity would be asserted rather than demonstrated: a nding from
one platform cannot be extended to social media by relabelling the object. A
radio-specic case narrows the claim and makes the conditions of transfer explicit.
The logic is analytical rather than statistical generalization. LOKLOK is
a plausibility probe for EST: if the specied architecture produces the predicted
trade-o under controlled assignment, the theory gains support within the model;
if it does not, the theory is challenged. The case is not a prevalence estimate for
platforms, nor a human treatment eect. The appropriate inferential target is the
mechanism, not the medium.
The pipeline follows this scope logic. The eld wave xes the population and
the radio-specic instruments. The qualitative stream supplies candidate design vo-
cabulary about listening, trust, participation, and correction; it is not a calibration
target. The BGE-M3 four-stream representation encodes quantitative, qualitative,
stimulus, and reference material, but the embedding is a pipeline feature, not ev-
idence of human delity. The ABM instantiates the eight cells with 500 personas
and 18 sessions, varying BRS, diversity, and echo control inside a radio-like feed;
the randomized-assignment triangulation then tests whether the estimated contrast
depends on assignment and interference. The outcomes remain SReval, SRcomp,
and engagement, which are meaningful for this case. Extending the pipeline to text,
image, or video platforms would require revalidated instruments, modality-specic
stimuli, and a new identication argument; it is not a relabelling exercise. Table 1.2

1.3
Key Terms and Units of Analysis
Students' ratings.
Audience evaluations, including stars and questionnaire scores; not academic
grades or demonstrated learning outcomes.
Perceived credibility.
A judgment of believability or trustworthiness, distinguished from content ac-
curacy, which requires an external assessment of the claims.
Engagement.
A family of behaviours or reports. A click, a completed listen, a comment,
and a self-reported interaction category are not interchangeable quantities.
Broadcaster score and broadcaster questionnaire.
The algorithmic BRS is a design object; the 11-item broadcaster-rating battery

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION
8
is an audience instrument. Reliability of the latter does not directly establish
accuracy or fairness of the former.
Observation.
The eld analysis uses 52 retained questionnaire records. An episode, a post,
a broadcaster, and a simulation run are dierent units. Their counts cannot
replace the number of independent respondents.
EST proposes mechanisms; LOKLOK species an architecture; the ques-
tionnaire describes audience judgments; and the simulation explores conditional
contrasts. These components belong together but warrant dierent conclusions.
1.4
The Research Problem
The original title, The Social Media Radio Innovation and its impact on University
Students Ratings, names the research problem rather than asserting that every im-
pact has already been causally identied. Student Rating refers to the student's
media competence and development; students' ratings of broadcasts refers to au-
dience evaluations. The eld survey measures the latter. Section 3.7 distinguishes
the human competence construct from the proposed computational extension. That
extension tests synthetic task performance and platform dynamics, with exploratory
NMLS-format responses; it does not supply a human competence eect.
The thesis addresses an integration problem identied in the reviewed liter-
ature. Accounts of broadcast authority, social trust, credibility, algorithmic cura-
tion, and constrained attention illuminate dierent parts of platform communica-
tion. EST brings them into a single proposed framework with explicit architectural

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION
9
and measurement commitments. This is an argument for a particular synthesis, not
proof that no earlier theory considered these relationships.
The empirical problem is how to distinguish a platform's reputation design
from audience judgments of that design and from independently assessed informa-
tion quality. The framework must specify what is measured, which relationships
are observed, and which claims require an intervention. The eld questionnaire and
model comparison address dierent parts of that problem and are reported sepa-
rately.
1.5
The Contribution of This Thesis
This thesis makes a single integrated contribution: an original theoretical frame-
work, Epistemic Systems Theory (EST), together with an epistemic governance
platform (LOKLOK) that implements selected mechanisms and species others for
prospective testing, an empirical evaluation that combines a measured eld wave
with a calibrated in-silico counterfactual experiment, and an evaluated set of survey
instruments. The framework is developed in Chapter 3; the platform is specied,
with its historical implementation account distinguished in Chapter 4; the empirical
evaluation is in Chapters 5 and 6.
Four components develop and examine the framework. First, a eld mea-
surement wave of 52 university students who listen to social-media radio while rid-
ing with Uber in the October 6th City area of Giza produced a survey battery
with reported internal consistency and factor-t diagnostics (Chapter 6). Second, a
calibrated two-arm in-silico experiment representing alternative platform rules esti-

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION
10
mated a model-conditional contrast between an epistemic-rst and an engagement-
rst architecture. Third, the 60 supplied rider accounts support a thematic analysis
and a 52-case paired joint display. Fourth, the LOKLOK implementation account
describes a Go backend, Flutter client, and web application. Their delity to the
reference equations must be established before the planned agent experiment; a
scalar production score is not automatically the theoretical BRS. The four-stream
BGE-M3 embedding is a pipeline feature, not the headline contribution: the source
ablation later shows that the semantic block is contextual, while the contrast is
carried by the mechanism and the state-outcome weights.
1.6
Research Questions
The thesis retains four theory-led questions, adds two mixed-methods questions, and
species a student-focused question for the extended design. These additions are
not retrospectively described as preregistered. RQ1RQ4 do not map one-to-one
onto its four propositions: RQ4 examines integration, whereas P4 motivates the
prospective task-performance comparison in H7 and RQ7.
1. RQ1 (Structural determination).
Do platform architecture, credibility
metrics, and content-ranking functions determine epistemic outcomes (per-
ceived quality, credibility, diversity) more than user-level characteristics do?
2. RQ2 (Diversity constraints).
Under the specied network and ranking
rules, do active diversity constraints alter concentration and engagement in
the directions proposed by EST-P2?
3. RQ3 (Psychometric accountability). To what extent do the consequential

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION
11
metrics of the platform, the Broadcaster Reputation Score (BRS) and the
survey instruments, meet published psychometric standards?
4. RQ4 (Integration). Do the epistemic constructs of EST behave as facets of
a single consolidated quality channel, both in the measured wave and in the
calibrated counterfactual experiment?
5. RQ5 (Audience experience). How do the rider records describe credibility,
listening value, participation, and platform experience?
6. RQ6 (Integration). Where do these accounts converge with, complement,
or challenge the paired questionnaire ratings?
7. RQ7 (Computational extension). How does assigned exposure to the spec-
ied LOKLOK congurations change evidence-anchored agents' task accuracy,
media production, and exposure relative to G0? If held-out human outcomes
are available, how accurately do the agents reproduce them?
1.7
Research Objectives
1. Develop EST with four formal propositions from which testable hypotheses
can be deduced (Chapter 3).
2. Specify and implement LOKLOK, an epistemic-rst social media radio plat-
form (Chapter 4).
3. Integrate the eld questionnaire with a transparent thematic analysis of rider
records to examine audience evaluations and measurement properties (Chap-
ter 5).
4. Calibrate an agent-based model to the measured wave and run a specied

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION
12
two-arm counterfactual experiment (Chapter 5).
5. Distinguish human Student Rating from broadcast evaluations and specify a
computational extension using independent task accuracy, with NMLS-format
responses as secondary synthetic diagnostics.
6. Evaluate the hypotheses and propositions and draw design and policy conclu-
sions (Chapter 6).
1.8
Hypotheses
Seven hypotheses organise the evaluation. H1 to H4 are primary in the thesis struc-
ture, not certied as prospectively registered tests; H5 and H6 are exploratory, while
H7 is formulated for the prospective computational extension. Their assessment
distinguishes eld associations, model results, and outcomes not directly measured.
Each hypothesis is mapped to a proposition of EST.
1. H1 (Structural credibility, EST-P1). Exposure to an epistemically archi-
tected interface is positively associated with perceived credibility and con-
dence.
2. H2 (Diversity mechanism, EST-P2). Architectural exposure increases the
perceived diversity of consumed content and reduces echo-driven repetition.
3. H3 (Psychometric validity, EST-P3).
The study instruments demon-
strate acceptable internal consistency, while structural validity is rigorously
examined rather than assumed.
4. H4 (EST integration, EST-P1 to P3). The epistemic measures form a
positive manifold consistent with one consolidated quality channel.

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION
13
5. H5 (DeGroot conformity, EST-P2, exploratory). Correction acceptance
and echo-persistence dynamics behave as conformity processes.
6. H6 (Scheduling and duration, EST-P1, exploratory). Listening persis-
tence is architecture-dependent and trades o against perceived quality.
7. H7
(Participatory
performance,
EST-P4;
prospective).
Under
matched model, content, network, and resource conditions, the specied
platform support improves agent claim-appraisal accuracy and evidence-based
contributions relative to the comparison conguration. Task accuracy is the
primary endpoint and production quality is secondary. This computational
hypothesis concerns observed outputs, not inferred human development.
The prospective LLM extension is a further methodological objective, not
a completed hypothesis test.
It will use consent-compatible qualitative anchors
to guide agents operating an isolated instance of LOKLOK, and will test synthetic
task performance, exposure, and production. Any additional claim of human delity
requires outcomes withheld from agent prompts; without them, inference remains
computational.
1.9
What the Student Ratings Mean
Student Rating is an umbrella term in this thesis, not a single number. Table 1.3
xes the meaning of each rating before the results are presented. The evaluative
Student Rating (SReval) is a 17 score built from the credibility and perceived-benet
items and scored through the GRM model. The competence-format Student Rating
(SRcomp) is a 0100 display built from the synthetic NMLS battery. Perceived benet

1.10
Scope and Delimitations
The measured wave is a cross-sectional questionnaire of 52 students who listen to
social media radio during rides with Uber in the October 6th City area, Giza. It is a
psychometric anchor, not a completed eld experiment. The causal contrast between
architectural congurations is evaluated in a calibrated in-silico experiment and is

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION
15
explicitly disclosed as such. The next platform-in-the-loop extension is a proposed
computational design specied in Chapter 5; a longitudinal human comparison re-
mains a separate future study, not a prerequisite for bounded computational claims.
Every claim in the results chapters is tied to the questionnaire, recorded qualitative
accounts, or the historical calibrated simulation; no result is asserted on the basis
of projected trajectories.
1.11
Thesis Structure
Chapter 2 reviews six epistemic dimensions of social media audio in the existing
literature. Chapter 3 develops EST and its four propositions. Chapter 4 species
the LOKLOK platform and its reported implementation boundaries.
Chapter 5
describes the mixed-methods eld study, historical calibrated model, and planned
LLM platform extension. Chapter 6 reports the results. Chapter 7 draws conclu-
sions, states limitations, and outlines the conrmatory pathway.
Chapter summary. Chapter 1 sets the question and the boundaries. The
thesis asks whether LOKLOK's design can improve epistemic quality without
destroying engagement, but it does not claim a causal eld eect. The mea-
sured wave anchors the problem; the simulation explores design implications.
The contribution is the integration of theory, measurement, and a reproducible
formal model, with explicit limits on what each evidence tier can support.
